Potential participants were screened to make sure that they were both citizens and residents of the UK or the US, aged between 18 to 35 (for younger adults) or 65 and 85 (for older adults), and are able to name at least one team either for NFL (National Football League; a professional league for American football in US) or Premier League (a professional league for soccer in UK; see the Procedure section for more details).
All participants gave informed consent before participation, and the experiment was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Economics and Social Sciences of the University of Tübingen.
Here, participants were asked to list as many teams from both leagues as possible in one minute each ("a listing task"); the league for which they started listing the teams was randomly assigned.
In the main experiment, participants completed the trivia question paradigm and the ECS, with the task order randomized for each participant.
The trivia question paradigm included 40 trials; after the 20th trial, participants were allowed to take a break.
Participants were instructed to provide their best guess for every question and were assured that their best guess was appreciated, even when they were uncertain about the answer.
Participants completed 3 practice trials about sports in general to familiarize themselves with the format before the task began.
All participants completed the OSpan task at the end of the experiment.
These findings are consistent with our expectation that participants had more knowledge about their domestic league compared to the foreign league.
Data from 32 participants were excluded because they met one or more of six preregistered exclusion criteria (see OSM).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants included 216 adults. The sample size was determined by an a priori power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) to achieve a 95% statistical power to detect smallsized effects of knowledge on curiosity (Cohen's f = 0.1) observed in previous studies (Wade & Kidd, 2019; Witherby & Carpenter, 2022). This sample size also ensured a 95% power to detect a small-to medium-sized effect (Cohen's f = 0.19) of age on trait curiosity and working memory.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Recent studies suggest that older adults maintain high levels of state curiosity when presented with epistemic materials, despite age-related declines in personality traits related to curiosity.

We hypothesized that this age-related preservation in state curiosity is explained by older adults' rich prior knowledge, given that knowledge acts as a key driver of state curiosity across the adult lifespan.
To test this idea, we conducted two experiments that examined older and younger adults' curiosity to learn the answers to questions in low-and high-knowledge domains.
Experiment 1 (N = 216) used learning materials characterized by large population-level differences in prior knowledge, but limited variation across age groups.
The results showed that prior knowledge substantially affects state curiosity, irrespective of age, while the effect of age on state curiosity was minimal.
Experiment 2 (N = 216) explicitly accounted for age differences in knowledge by orthogonalizing the effects of knowledge and age.

We found that relative to younger adults, older adults experienced stronger curiosity for high-knowledge domains, whereas in other domains where younger adults were more knowledgeable, older adults experienced weaker curiosity relative to younger adults.
Such age-related differences in curiosity were mediated by age-related differences in knowledge.
These findings point to the important role of prior knowledge in curiosity across younger and older adults, extending theoretical notions on curiosity.
Our results also suggest that previously observed age differences in state curiosity might be partly attributable to age-related differences in knowledge.

text.text: However, previous studies on state curiosity and aging did not systematically control for prior knowledge; thus, little is known about the role of prior knowledge in older adults' epistemic curiosity.
In the present study, we examine the role that prior knowledge plays in state epistemic curiosity in older and younger adults.
We hypothesize that prior knowledge positively affects epistemic curiosity, regardless of age.

We also hypothesize that the age-related differences in epistemic curiosity are at least partly due to age-related differences in knowledge; thus, we expect that older and younger adults show similar levels of epistemic curiosity after controlling for knowledge.
To address these hypotheses, we conducted two experiments.
In both experiments, older and younger adults were presented with trivia questions from one domain in which they had high prior knowledge and another domain in which they had low prior knowledge.
Experiment 1 used learning materials characterized by large population-level differences in prior knowledge, but limited variation across age groups.

Specifically, we tested participants from the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US), and asked them to indicate their curiosity about questions in two different domains: soccer and American football.

American football has been the most popular sport to follow for American people across all age groups (Jones, 2024); in contrast, soccer (football) is the most popular sport for British people to follow, irrespective of age (YouGov, n.d.).
Thus, British people are expected to know more about soccer than American football (and vice versa for US people), irrespective of age.

Based on our hypothesis that prior knowledge is a key factor responsible for age differences in curiosity, we expected a significant interaction between participants' nationality and knowledge domain in curiosity, irrespective of age; in other words, British participants should report stronger curiosity for questions about soccer than American football (and vice versa for US participants).
Experiment 2 aimed to extend Experiment 1 by treating knowledge and age as orthogonal factors.

Specifically, we used questions about two groups of celebrities: a) those known well by younger generations but not by older generations, and b) those known well by older generations but not by younger generations.
We expected that older adults, relative to younger adults, would show higher levels of curiosity about celebrities famous to older generations.
In contrast, the pattern should be reversed for the other celebrities (those famous for younger generations), such that older adults should show lower levels of curiosity relative to younger adults.
In Experiment 1, we recruited older adults and younger adults from the US and UK and presented them with a series of questions from two domains: soccer and American football.
For each question, participants first rated their curiosity to learn the answer, and then their interest in the answer once they saw it.

As described earlier, we expected that participants from the UK would report higher curiosity ratings for soccer than American football, while participants from the US would report higher curiosity ratings for American football than soccer.
To test this prediction, we selected learning materials that showed large knowledge differences based on country of origin, but only limited age-related differences.

While it still remained plausible that older adults generally possessed more knowledge than younger adults and, consequently, reported higher state curiosity, we expected that the size of this main effect should be smaller than the effect size of the interaction.

To ensure that participants knew more about a sport domain famous for their country than the other domain, we asked all participants to generate as many teams as possible for American football and soccer (thereafter called a listing task).

Given that younger adults outperform older adults in this type of fluency task due to the age-related cognitive declines (Lanting et al., 2009; Tomer & Levin, 1993), this task is not suited to examine age-related differences in knowledge.

text.text: The results from Experiment 1 indicate that prior knowledge positively predicts epistemic curiosity across older and younger adults.
While we also found a significant main effect of age on curiosity, its effect size was significantly smaller than the effect size for the interaction between nationality and domain.
These results are in line with our hypothesis that age-related changes in prior knowledge serve as a key in explaining age-related differences in epistemic curiosity.
However, there are also several limitations.
First, we focused on one particular domain (football) and excluded participants who failed to list any teams from the NFL or the Premier League.
Therefore, the results may be specific to individuals who are interested in sports, limiting generalizability.

Second, because we did not treat age and knowledge as orthogonal factors in our design, it was unclear whether the differences in state curiosity between older and younger adults could be attributed to knowledge differences.
Experiment 2 aimed to address these limitations by introducing several changes.
First, we used a new set of materials, namely, questions about celebrities.

We created stimulus sets comprised of two groups of celebrities to examine the effects of knowledge driven by age: those primarily known by the younger generation and those primarily known by the older generation.
This enables us to treat age group and knowledge level as orthogonal factors, allowing us to isolate the effects of knowledge from the effects of age.
Second, we obtained more detailed measures of participants' prior knowledge about each stimulus by explicitly asking all participants to rate their familiarity with each celebrity.
People should feel higher levels of familiarity for celebrities they know well than those they know little about (Reder et al., 2013).
text.formatted: People should feel higher levels of familiarity for celebrities they know well than those they know little about <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Reder et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, this allowed us to check if our manipulation worked as intended (e.g., if older adults are familiar with one group of celebrities over the other) and examine whether prior knowledge predicts curiosity on a trial-to-trial basis.
Lastly, we incorporated a behavioral measure of epistemic curiosity (i.e., information seeking) to complement subjective curiosity ratings.
Similar to Experiment 1, we predicted knowledge to positively affect state curiosity and information seeking across age.

Specifically, we hypothesized that for celebrities known by older generations, older adults would show higher levels of curiosity and information seeking behavior than do younger adults; in contrast, for celebrities known by younger generations, older adults should show lower levels of curiosity and information seeking behavior than younger adults.
Lastly, we predicted that younger adults would score higher on trait curiosity compared to older adults.

To further examine whether prior knowledge explains age differences in epistemic curiosity, we conducted a non-preregistered mediation analysis examining whether the effect of age on state curiosity was mediated by familiarity ratings.

Here, familiarity was used as a proxy for prior knowledge and was operationalized as a within-subject difference score: the average familiarity rating for celebrities in the known-by-old domain minus the average familiarity rating for celebrities in the known-by-young domain for each participant, i.e., Δ familiarity.

State curiosity was operationalized similarly: the average curiosity rating for known-by-old celebrities minus the average curiosity rating for known-by-young celebrities for each participant, i.e., Δ state curiosity.
Consequently, positive values reflected relatively greater curiosity or familiarity for known-by-old compared to known-by-young domains, whereas negative values reflected the opposite pattern.
Age group was effect coded (1: old, -1: young).

text.text: Given the importance of curiosity in old age, a growing number of studies investigated factors that affect epistemic curiosity in older adults (Sobczak et al., 2025; Swirsky et al., 2021; Swirsky & Spaniol, 2024b; Yagi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Given the importance of curiosity in old age, a growing number of studies investigated factors that affect epistemic curiosity in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sobczak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Swirsky et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Swirsky & Spaniol, 2024b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Yagi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, existing research does not provide a clear idea about how and why older adults report stronger levels of state epistemic curiosity for a specific piece of information relative to younger adults.
The present study aimed to address this issue by focusing on the role of prior knowledge.
Across two experiments, both older and younger adults reported higher curiosity ratings for highknowledge domains than for low-knowledge domains.
This effect of knowledge was significantly larger than the main effect of age in Experiment 1.

In addition, in Experiment 2, we found that older adults experience stronger epistemic curiosity only for high-knowledge domains; in other domains, where younger adults were more knowledgeable, older adults experienced weaker curiosity relative to younger adults.
Furthermore, we demonstrated that age differences in curiosity across those domains were partially mediated by familiarity ratings.
These results are in line with our hypothesis that age-related differences in state curiosity might be partly attributable to age-related differences in prior knowledge.

Previous studies have repeatedly indicated that older adults experience stronger levels of epistemic curiosity relative to younger adults (Fastrich et al., 2024; Galli et al., 2018; Whatley et al., 2025).

text.text: The present study extends these prior studies by examining state epistemic curiosity across both low and high prior knowledge domains.

We found that the effect of prior knowledge on state curiosity occurs across older and younger adults, different materials (those on football and those on celebrities) and measures (curiosity ratings and information seeking).

We also demonstrated positive associations between curiosity and multiple proxies of prior knowledge, including confidence and familiarity, although these relationships weakened at higher levels of both measures.

The role of knowledge in explaining age differences in state curiosity may also be relevant in interpreting findings from another study on curiosity and aging; Fastrich et al. (2024) reported that older adults' information-seeking style is more specific (i.e., exploring facts within one topic), whereas that of younger adults is more diverse (i.e., exploring facts by switching between topics).

text.text: Building on the reward-learning framework of knowledge acquisition (Murayama, 2022), one would expect individuals to be more curious about a topic, and to search for more information about it, when their knowledge increases.

text.text: Similar to how increasing knowledge in older adults may account for the apparent age differences in state curiosity, it may also evoke a change in information-seeking styles; as knowledge in certain areas increases with age, information-seeking might shift from more diverse to more specific in those areas.
In addition, in line with previous studies (Robinson et al., 2017; Whatley et al., 2025; Wiegand et al., 2025), we found that older adults scored lower on trait curiosity than younger adults.

text.text: This age-related decline in trait curiosity is consistent with several lifespan theories of human motivation, which suggest a decline in acquiring knowledge with increasing age.

For instance, socioemotional selectivity theory suggests that, in older adulthood, less priority is given to goals such as knowledge acquisition and more to emotionally meaningful pursuits (Carstensen, 2021; Carstensen et al., 1999).

text.text: The suggestions from these theories, together with previous findings on age-related changes in trait curiosity and our own results, make the findings on state curiosity even more intriguing: in the same participant groups in which trait curiosity decreases with age, state curiosity appears to increase (Whatley et al., 2025).

text.text: Our findings may provide insights into this contrasting age-related pattern of state and trait curiosity.
Specifically, this pattern may be explained by differences in how state and trait curiosity are operationalized.

Measures on trait curiosity include questions on participants' information-seeking behavior in their everyday life; in contrast, state epistemic curiosity was typically assessed by asking the subjective feeling of curiosity in response to a specific learning material (e.g., trivia questions).
In Experiment 2, we included a behavioral measure of information seeking for each celebrity.
Here, we found that older adults searched for less additional information than younger adults.
Swirsky and Spaniol (2024) already showed agerelated differences in the correlation between curiosity and information seeking.

Our study extends these previous findings and suggests that age affects self-reported measures of curiosity and information seeking differently, which might explain why older adults score lower on trait curiosity questionnaires compared to younger adults.

This lower rate of information seeking among older adults is consistent with the socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen, 2021) and may be due to the age-related increases in cognitive costs associated with such behavior (Hess, 2014).

text.text: Our results also provide insights into the relation between curiosity and interest, two constructs that are highly related to each other.
As observed in previous studies, we found that curiosity and interest were highly correlated across participants when we assessed them for each question in Experiment 1.
However, our item-level analysis showed that they were more strongly related for the high-knowledge domain than for the low-knowledge domain (see OSM).
These results are in line with previous notions that interest is more relevant to knowledge than curiosity (Hidi & Renninger, 2020).

text.text: Future research needs to examine the dynamic interplay among these factors across the adult lifespan.
There are a few important limitations with the present study.
First, one concern is the potential generalizability.
Although we attempted to address this issue by conducting two experiments using different sets of materials, both sets assessed only one topic, namely, football and celebrities.

The generalizability of the findings may therefore be restricted to similar types of content or to participants who are particularly interested in these topics, as participants were aware of the topics before choosing to participate.
We also only focused on participant groups from the UK and the US.
Furthermore, the ecological validity of the trivia question paradigm may be limited.

In real-world settings, satisfying curiosity usually requires effort and occurs in an open-ended fashion where one can freely explore (Gottlieb et al., 2013; Murayama, 2022; Murayama et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 2026).

text.text: Future research needs to examine the role that knowledge plays in curiosity across adulthood in more naturalistic settings.
Another important question concerns our measures of prior knowledge.
In the present study, we used two domains, where we expected a clear group difference in the amount of prior knowledge to clearly observe its effect on state curiosity.
This experimental manipulation was complemented by the listing task (in Experiment 1) and familiarity ratings (in Experiment 2) that aimed to assess participants' knowledge of the two domains.
In Experiment 1, US participants were able to list more NFL teams than Premier League teams (and vice versa for UK participants).
In Experiment 2, participants reported stronger curiosity and chose to engage in information seeking more for celebrities that they felt more familiar with than other celebrities.
Our mediation analyses further revealed that both of these knowledge measures predicted curiosity.
Given this comparable pattern across the two different measures of knowledge, the effects of knowledge observed in the present study were unlikely due to the specific measures we used.
However, it is difficult, if not impossible, to fully assess one's knowledge and therefore these tasks likely have assessed only a part of one's knowledge.
In addition, neither of the measures directly assessed the amount of knowledge gaps, which should predict curiosity according to theoretical notions (Loewenstein, 1994; Murayama, 2022).

text.text: Future studies should develop fine-grained measures of prior knowledge to reliably assess one's knowledge and to assess how it affects curiosity across the adult lifespan.
Lastly, we did not find significant differences in working memory performance between younger and older adults.

Although the effects of age on working memory were not always observed (Jaroslawska & Rhodes, 2019; Verhaeghen et al., 2003), younger adults typically outperform older adults in such tasks (Alloway & Alloway, 2013; Hartshorne & Germine, 2015).

text.text: The lack of significant differences may be due to several factors.
First, we excluded older adults with signs of cognitive decline during the screening phase.
While this helped us to ensure that all participants had the ability to consent, we may have had a sample of older adults with potentially, on average, higher working memory spans.

Second, because of time constraints, a shortened version of the OSpan task was used to assess working memory (Oswald et al., 2015), which may not have been sensitive enough to detect age differences compared to the full version or to using multiple shorter versions (Foster et al., 2015; Oswald et al., 2015).

text.text: Third, older adults on platforms like Prolific might have higher cognitive abilities than those who would participate in lab-based experiments.

However, it should be noted that we replicated previous findings that older adults show poorer performance in a fluency task in Experiment 1 (Jaroslawska & Rhodes, 2019; Verhaeghen et al., 2003), and that older adults responded more slowly than younger adults in both experiments (Fricker, 2005; Ratcliff, 2008; Yan & Tourangeau, 2008), suggesting that there were age-related declines in cognitive abilities even in our participants.

text.text: Nevertheless, it is important for future research to examine whether and how the results are replicable in other samples who show clear age-related declines in working memory capacities.
We often associate curiosity primarily with children and hold a negative stereotype that curiosity decreases in adulthood.
However, our study indicates that both younger and older adults report strong curiosity for something unknown as long as they have relevant prior knowledge.

Given that older adults generally have a richer knowledge base than younger adults, these results suggest that older adults may, in general, experience even higher curiosity in life relative to younger adults.

By highlighting the role of accumulated knowledge over the lifespan in sustaining epistemic curiosity, our findings offer a positive view of curiosity in later adulthood and highlight the importance of knowledge as a key driver of curiosity across the lifespan.
